nodeData.note: A practical course on growing tomato organically, from variety choice and nursery to nutrition, pests, diseases, harvest and markets. Notes on capsicum and chilli, which belong to the same family, are at the end.

children.note: What tomato is, how varieties differ and which are commonly grown in Kenya and India.

Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) belongs to the Solanaceae, together with potato, capsicum, chilli, eggplant and African nightshade (managu). They share many pests and diseases, so treat them as one group in rotation.

manas.q: Which crops share the tomato family, and why does it matter for rotation?

children.note: Determinate (bush) types stop growing at a flower cluster and ripen their fruit over a shorter period, which suits open fields. Indeterminate types keep growing and fruiting for months and need staking or trellising; they are typical in greenhouses.

manas.q: What is the difference between determinate and indeterminate tomatoes?

children.note: Seed of open-pollinated varieties can be saved and replanted. F1 hybrids are more uniform and often carry disease resistance, but saved seed does not breed true, so new seed is bought each season.

Widely grown open-pollinated types include Cal J, Rio Grande and Money Maker; many farmers use F1 hybrids such as Anna F1 (greenhouse) and Kilele F1. Ask local extension which resist the wilts and viruses in your area.

Public-sector varieties from ICAR institutes are widely used; for example IIHR Bengaluru released Arka Rakshak with combined resistance to leaf curl virus, bacterial wilt and early blight. State universities list varieties for each zone.

Letters on seed packets show bred-in resistance, for example V (Verticillium), F (Fusarium races), N (root-knot nematode), ToMV (tomato mosaic) and TYLCV (yellow leaf curl). Choosing the right codes is the cheapest disease control.

manas.q: What do letters like V, F and N on a tomato seed packet mean?

children.note: Organic standards ask for organically produced seed where it is available; otherwise untreated conventional seed is usually allowed. Seed dressed with synthetic fungicides or insecticides is not allowed.
Tomato is a warm-season crop that dislikes frost, very high heat and long leaf wetness.
Growth is best in warm days and mild nights. Fruit set fails when nights are cold or days are very hot, because pollen is damaged; flowers then drop without forming fruit.

manas.q: Why do tomato flowers drop in very hot weather?

children.note: Long periods of wet leaves favour late blight, early blight and bacterial spots. Many farmers plant so that the crop grows in the drier season with irrigation, or use rain shelters and greenhouses.
Best on deep, well-drained loams rich in organic matter, with pH around 6.0–6.8. Heavy, waterlogged soils lead to root rots and wilts.

manas.q: What soil pH range suits tomato?

children.note: Avoid fields where tomato, potato, capsicum or eggplant grew in recent seasons, and any field where bacterial wilt was seen. Soil-borne wilts survive for years.
Healthy seedlings and a clean field prevent most problems before they start.
Leave a break of at least three seasons without any nightshade crop. Good preceding crops are cereals, legumes or onions; a legume also leaves nitrogen.

manas.q: How long should a field rest from nightshade crops before tomato?

children.note: Raise seedlings in raised beds or trays filled with fresh, well-made compost mixed with soil or coco peat. Trays give each seedling its own root ball and less transplant shock.
In the hot season, wet the bed and cover it tightly with clear plastic for four to six weeks. The heat kills many weed seeds, fungi and nematodes in the top layer.

manas.q: How does soil solarisation work?

children.note: Cover the nursery with fine insect netting. This keeps out whiteflies that carry leaf curl virus and Tuta absoluta moths, so seedlings go to the field clean.

manas.q: Why should a tomato nursery be covered with insect net?

children.note: Reduce watering for about a week before transplanting to toughen seedlings. Transplant at four to six true leaves, in the evening or on a cloudy day, and water in at once.
Wider spacing and staking keep fruit off the soil and let air move, which reduces blights. Indeterminate types are tied to stakes or strings; determinate types may be left bushy or lightly supported.
A layer of dry grass or straw stops rain splashing soil (and early blight spores) onto lower leaves, holds moisture, cools the soil and suppresses weeds.
On indeterminate plants remove side shoots while small, and later remove the lowest leaves that touch the soil. Prune on dry days and clean tools between plants.
Tomato is a heavy feeder. Build soil before planting, add biofertilizers at each stage and feed steadily during fruiting.
Fruit takes away large amounts of potassium and nitrogen, plus calcium, magnesium and phosphorus. Potassium is linked to fruit colour, firmness and taste.

manas.q: Which nutrient does tomato fruit remove in especially large amounts?

children.note: Work well-made compost or rotted farmyard manure into the beds or planting holes before transplanting. Fresh manure can burn roots and carry pathogens, so use it only after composting.
A legume green manure such as sunn hemp, mucuna or lablab, cut and worked in before flowering, adds nitrogen and organic matter. Sunn hemp is also reported to reduce root-knot nematodes.
Coat seed with Trichoderma or Pseudomonas fluorescens before sowing to protect against damping-off. Do not mix these with chemical seed dressings.
Dip seedling roots for a short time in a slurry of Azospirillum, PSB and Pseudomonas in clean water, then plant at once in moist soil, out of direct sun.

manas.q: Which biofertilizers are commonly used as a tomato seedling root dip?

children.note: Mix Azotobacter or Azospirillum, PSB and KMB (or a bio-NPK consortium) with compost and place it near the roots at planting. Biofertilizers add to compost; they do not replace it.
Tomato forms mycorrhiza readily. Inoculating the nursery can improve phosphorus and water uptake, especially in low-P soils.
Side-dress compost or vermicompost at flowering and again during fruit set. Liquid manures or compost teas every one to two weeks keep feeding steady.
Organic options include wood ash in moderation (it raises pH), naturally mined potassium sulphate, and composted banana stems and crop residues.
Excess nitrogen gives large dark leaves, few flowers, late fruit and soft growth that attracts aphids and blight.

manas.q: What happens if tomato gets too much nitrogen?

children.note: A dark, sunken patch at the bottom of the fruit. It comes from poor calcium supply to the fruit, usually caused by irregular watering rather than a lack of soil calcium; steady watering and mulch are the main cure.

manas.q: What is the main cause of blossom-end rot in tomato?

Opens the map on making and using compost.
Opens the map on Trichoderma.
Opens the map on Azospirillum.
Even moisture is the key to good fruit set and sound fruit.
Drip irrigation keeps leaves dry, saves water and allows filtered liquid manures and biofertilizers to be applied through the line.
Water needs are highest from flowering through fruit enlargement. Stress at this time causes flower drop and small fruit.
Long dry spells followed by heavy watering or rain make fruit split, and also cause blossom-end rot.

manas.q: What causes tomato fruit to crack?

children.note: The main insects and mites of tomato, with symptoms and organic control. Use the doors for full pest maps.
A small moth from South America (now also named Phthorimaea absoluta). It reached North Africa in 2008 and has since spread through most of Africa, including Kenya, and into India.
Pale, see-through blotches (mines) in leaves with dark droppings inside, which later dry brown. Larvae also bore into stems and fruit, leaving small holes, often near the calyx.

manas.q: What does Tuta absoluta damage look like on tomato leaves?

children.note: Sex pheromone traps catch male moths and give early warning. Many traps per field (mass trapping) can lower numbers, especially in greenhouses.
Use clean, netted seedlings, pick and destroy mined leaves and bored fruit in sealed bags, remove crop residues at once, and leave a gap between crops.
Allowed options include Bt and spinosad on young larvae, neem, and predatory mirid bugs used in Mediterranean greenhouses. Mirids and parasitoids are central to biological control worldwide.

links.label: 📄 Source: Annual Review of Entomology 2018 (Tuta absoluta review)

children.note: icipe found that tomato plants colonised by some Beauveria and Trichoderma strains suffered less leafmining (lab/screenhouse stage). icipe has also released a parasitic wasp, Dolichogenidea gelechiidivoris, in Kenya.
Opens the map on caterpillar pests, including Tuta.

Tiny white flies under leaves; Bemisia tabaci spreads tomato yellow leaf curl virus. Use netted nurseries, yellow sticky traps, neem or soap sprays, Beauveria, and in greenhouses parasitic wasps (Encarsia, Eretmocerus).

manas.q: Which tomato virus is spread by whiteflies?

children.note: Thrips scar leaves and fruit and spread tomato spotted wilt virus; aphids cause curling. Use blue (thrips) and yellow (aphids) sticky traps, conserve predators and use neem or soap.
Fine yellow speckles on leaves, then webbing, in hot dry weather. Spray water under leaves, release predatory mites, or use sulphur (allowed, but not in heat or with oil sprays).
Helicoverpa armigera caterpillars eat round holes into green and ripe fruit. Use pheromone traps, Bt or Helicoverpa NPV virus on young larvae, and in India marigold rows as a trap crop.
Roots show knots (galls); plants are stunted and wilt in the heat. Rotate, use N-resistant varieties, add plenty of compost and grow sunn hemp or marigold before tomato.
Opens the map on aphids, whiteflies, thrips and mites.
Opens the map on plant-parasitic nematodes.
The main tomato diseases and how organic growers prevent them. No disease can be cured once it is in the vascular system; prevention is everything.

Caused by the water mould Phytophthora infestans in cool, wet weather. Dark water-soaked patches spread fast on leaves and stems, with white growth underneath on humid mornings; fruit get firm brown patches.

manas.q: Which weather favours tomato late blight?

children.note: Plant away from potatoes, use tolerant varieties, stake, space and remove lower leaves, and remove infected plants at once. Copper sprays are allowed in organic farming within limits; Bacillus-based products are preventive only.
Alternaria fungus: brown spots with rings like a target, starting on the oldest leaves. Mulch, rotate, remove lower leaves and avoid wetting the leaves.

manas.q: How can early blight be told apart from late blight?

children.note: Ralstonia bacteria block the water vessels; plants collapse while still green. A cut stem in clear water releases milky threads (ooze test). There is no cure: remove plants, rotate with non-hosts, graft onto resistant rootstock.

manas.q: How do you confirm bacterial wilt in the field?

children.note: Leaves yellow, often on one side, and the inside of the stem turns brown. Use resistant (F) varieties, Trichoderma-enriched compost and long rotations.
Yellow leaf curl (whitefly), spotted wilt (thrips) and mosaic viruses (contact and seed) cannot be cured. Control the vectors, use resistant varieties and pull out infected plants early.
A newer virus that spreads on hands, tools and seed and breaks older mosaic resistance. Many countries treat it as a quarantine pest; use certified seed and strict hygiene.

manas.q: How does tomato brown rugose fruit virus spread?

children.note: Seedlings collapse at soil level. Use fresh media, avoid overwatering and crowding, and treat seed or media with Trichoderma.
Opens the map on blights and leaf spots.
Opens the map on Fusarium, Verticillium and bacterial wilts.
Opens the map on plant viruses and their vectors.
Opens the map on bacterial spots, cankers and soft rots.
Weeds compete hard in the first weeks and also shelter pests and viruses.
Keep the crop clean for the first several weeks after transplanting; later, the canopy and mulch shade weeds out.
Black nightshade, Datura and other wild Solanaceae host Tuta, whiteflies, viruses and wilts. Remove them from in and around the field.

manas.q: Why remove wild nightshade weeds around tomato?

children.note: In some regions (for example parts of India and the Mediterranean) the parasitic weed Orobanche attaches to tomato roots. Pull its shoots before they seed and rotate with non-hosts.
Use mulch, a stale seedbed (let weeds sprout, then hoe them) and shallow hand weeding. Herbicides are not allowed in organic production.
Opens the map on organic weed management.
Careful picking and handling decide how much of the crop reaches the buyer.
Fruit goes from mature green to breaker (first colour), pink and red. For distant markets pick at the breaker or pink stage; for nearby markets pick riper.

manas.q: At which stage should tomatoes be picked for a distant market?

children.note: Harvest in the morning, keep the calyx on, and place fruit in shallow crates rather than sacks so they do not bruise.
Sort out damaged and diseased fruit at once and keep the rest in shade. Rotten fruit left in the field feeds Tuta and fruit diseases.
Unripe tomatoes suffer chilling injury in a cold fridge and then ripen poorly. Keep them cool but not cold.
A simple charcoal or brick cooling chamber kept wet lowers temperature and keeps humidity high, extending shelf life without electricity.
How organic tomatoes are sold and what rules apply.
Organic tomatoes cannot receive synthetic fertilizers (such as DAP or CAN), synthetic insecticides or fungicides, or herbicides. Copper and sulphur are allowed within limits.

manas.q: Name two inputs not allowed on organic tomatoes.

children.note: East Africa uses the East African Organic Products Standard (EAS 456), India the NPOP, and the EU its organic regulation. Groups selling locally can use Participatory Guarantee Systems (PGS).
Buyers test for pesticide residues against maximum residue limits (MRLs). Keep records of every input, including allowed ones like copper.
Staggered planting every few weeks gives a steady harvest and avoids selling everything when prices crash.
Sweet pepper (capsicum) and chilli are Solanaceae like tomato, so most of this guide applies.
Do not follow tomato, potato or eggplant with capsicum or chilli: they share bacterial wilt, Phytophthora, viruses, thrips and mites.
Peppers need more warmth than tomato and are very sensitive to waterlogging; raised beds and greenhouses are common for capsicum.
Upward or downward curling of chilli leaves is caused by thrips, mites and leaf curl virus together. Manage vectors, use netted nurseries and remove infected plants early.
Colletotrichum fungus causes sunken, dark spots on ripening fruit. Use clean seed, remove infected fruit and avoid wet foliage.
Thaumatotibia leucotreta larvae bore into pepper fruit. It is a quarantine pest for the EU, so Kenyan exports of capsicum and chilli need strict field control and inspection.

manas.q: Why does false codling moth matter for Kenyan capsicum exports?

nodeData.note: A practical course on growing kale (sukuma wiki), cabbage, cauliflower and broccoli organically. They are close relatives with the same needs, pests and diseases, so they are managed as one crop group.

children.note: Which brassicas are covered and how they differ.
Kale, collards, cabbage, cauliflower and broccoli are all forms of Brassica oleracea, in the cabbage family (Brassicaceae, crucifers). Treat them as one group in rotation.

manas.q: Why are kale, cabbage, cauliflower and broccoli treated as one group in rotation?

children.note: The kale of East Africa is a collard-type Brassica oleracea grown for its leaves, which are picked one by one over many months. Its Swahili name means "push the week".

manas.q: How is sukuma wiki harvested differently from cabbage?

children.note: Common choices include Southern Georgia (collard) and Thousand-headed kale, plus newer F1 hybrids. Ethiopian kale (Brassica carinata, kanzira) is a related traditional leafy vegetable.
Grown for its tight head of leaves. In Kenya Copenhagen Market (open-pollinated) and F1 hybrids such as Gloria F1 are common; in India Golden Acre and Pride of India are well known.
Grown for the white curd, a mass of undeveloped flower stalks. Indian varieties are grouped as early, mid and late (snowball) types, because each forms curds only within its own temperature range.

manas.q: Why are Indian cauliflower varieties grouped into early, mid and late types?

children.note: Grown for its green head of unopened flower buds. After the main head is cut, side shoots give smaller extra heads.
Brassicas are cool-season crops that need steady growth.
Cabbage, cauliflower and broccoli grow best in cool to mild weather. Heat gives loose, bitter heads and yellow, ricey curds; kale tolerates a wider range.

manas.q: What does hot weather do to cauliflower curds and cabbage heads?

children.topic: Where they grow in East Africa
children.note: Cabbage, cauliflower and broccoli do best in the cooler highlands. Kale is grown almost everywhere there is water, including peri-urban plots.
Fertile, well-drained loam rich in organic matter, with pH about 6.0–7.0. Acid, wet soils favour clubroot.

manas.q: Which soil condition favours clubroot?

children.note: Avoid fields with recent brassicas or with clubroot or black rot in the past.
Clean seed, clean seedlings and long rotation prevent the worst brassica diseases.
Keep three to four seasons between brassica crops in the same soil, and control cruciferous weeds in between, because clubroot and black rot persist.

manas.q: How long a break between brassica crops is advised?

children.note: Black rot and Alternaria are carried on seed. Buy tested seed or use a carefully controlled hot-water seed treatment, then dry the seed.
Use raised beds or trays with fresh compost-based media, sow thinly and cover with fine insect net against diamondback moth, aphids and flea beetles.
Transplant at four to six true leaves. Discard seedlings with swollen roots (clubroot), black-veined leaves (black rot) or stunted, purple growth.
Cabbage and cauliflower need room for heads; kale is often planted a little closer for leaf harvest. Good spacing lets leaves dry and reduces downy mildew and black rot.

Rows of Indian mustard around or within cabbage attract diamondback moth and aphids away from the main crop. Winter cress (Barbarea) is studied as a "dead-end" trap: moths lay eggs on it but larvae die.

manas.q: What is a dead-end trap crop?

links.label: 📄 Source: Molecules 2019 (saponins and Barbarea trap crop)

children.note: Mixing brassicas with onion, garlic, coriander or flowering borders can host natural enemies and confuse pests; results vary, so treat it as one tool among many.
Dry grass mulch keeps soil moist and cool, reduces splash of soil-borne disease and suppresses weeds.
Brassicas are hungry for nitrogen, sulphur and potassium and are sensitive to boron and molybdenum shortage.
Leaves and heads take up large amounts of nitrogen and potassium, and more sulphur than most crops; sulphur forms the mustard-oil compounds (glucosinolates) that give brassicas their taste.
Work in plenty of well-made compost or rotted manure before transplanting. A previous legume or green manure adds nitrogen.
Treat seed with Trichoderma or Pseudomonas against damping-off, and dip seedling roots in Azospirillum or Azotobacter with PSB before planting.
Mix N-fixing bacteria, PSB and KMB (or a bio-NPK consortium) with compost at planting. These add to compost and manure; they do not replace them.
Brassicas do not form mycorrhiza, so mycorrhizal inoculants do not help them directly. Use them on the crops that follow instead.

manas.q: Do mycorrhizal inoculants help cabbage and kale?

children.note: Because leaves are picked for months, side-dress compost or vermicompost every few weeks and give liquid manure or compost tea regularly.
Compost, manures and gypsum supply sulphur; gypsum also adds calcium without changing pH much.
Lack of boron causes hollow, cracked stems in cabbage and broccoli and brown patches in cauliflower curds. Compost helps; small doses of approved boron sources correct it, but excess is toxic.

manas.q: What sign shows boron deficiency in cauliflower or broccoli?

children.note: In acid soils cauliflower can lack molybdenum, giving narrow, strap-like leaves (whiptail). Liming acid soil releases molybdenum.

manas.q: What is whiptail in cauliflower?

children.note: Brown leaf edges inside cabbage heads come from poor calcium movement during fast growth, often with uneven watering. Steady water matters more than extra calcium.
Agricultural lime or dolomite raises pH, supplies calcium and helps against clubroot. Lime well before planting and test soil first.

children.note: Opens the map on nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
Opens the map on manures and organic fertilizers.
Opens the map on Azotobacter.
Brassicas need steady moisture from transplanting to harvest.
Dry spells give tough, bitter leaves and small heads. Drip or careful furrow irrigation with mulch works well.
A heavy watering or rain after drought makes mature cabbage heads split. Water evenly and harvest heads on time.

manas.q: Why do cabbage heads split?

children.note: Overhead watering spreads black rot and downy mildew. Water at soil level and in the morning.
Main insect pests of brassicas, their symptoms and organic control. Use the doors for full pest maps.
Plutella xylostella is the most destructive brassica pest worldwide. Small green larvae wriggle backwards and drop on a silk thread when touched.
Young larvae mine leaves; older ones eat from below, leaving the upper skin as clear "windows", then holes. They also feed in growing points and heads.

manas.q: What feeding damage does diamondback moth leave on cabbage leaves?

children.note: DBM has become resistant to many insecticides and was the first insect to develop resistance to Bt in the field. Rotate products and rely on natural enemies.

manas.q: Which pest was the first to develop field resistance to Bt?

links.label: 📄 Source: PLOS Pathogens 2020 (Bt resistance in diamondback moth)

children.note: Parasitic wasps such as Diadegma and Cotesia can keep DBM low when broad-spectrum sprays are avoided. icipe introduced Diadegma semiclausum to the Kenyan highlands for this purpose.
Use netted nurseries, pheromone traps for monitoring, mustard trap crops, and Bt or spinosad on young larvae. Rain or sprinkler water also washes off and kills small larvae.
Opens the map on caterpillar pests, including DBM.
Cabbage webworm (Hellula), cabbage head caterpillar (Crocidolomia), loopers and cabbage white butterflies eat leaves and bore into hearts. Hand-pick egg masses and use Bt.
Brevicoryne brassicae forms dense grey, waxy colonies that curl leaves and contaminate heads. Encourage ladybirds and parasitoids, avoid excess nitrogen, and spray soap or neem on colonies.

manas.q: How can cabbage aphid be recognised?

children.note: Tiny jumping beetles make many small round holes in seedlings. Use insect net on nurseries and young plants and keep plants growing fast.
In hot, dry areas of Africa and India this small black-and-orange bug sucks seedlings until they wilt. Irrigate, hand-collect, and remove crop residues.
Grey caterpillars cut young transplants at soil level at night. Check plants at dawn, dig out larvae near cut plants and use collars.
Opens the map on aphids, whiteflies and other sucking pests.
Opens the map on beetle pests, including flea beetles.
Opens the map on cutworms and other soil pests.
Main brassica diseases and how organic growers prevent them.
Caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris. Yellow V-shaped patches start at leaf edges and point inward, with blackened veins; it is seed-borne and spreads by water splash.

manas.q: What are the typical symptoms of black rot on cabbage?

children.note: Use clean or hot-water-treated seed, rotate for three to four years, remove crucifer weeds and infected leaves, and avoid overhead watering. Copper is allowed within limits but only slows spread.
Caused by Plasmodiophora brassicae. Roots swell into clubs, plants wilt on hot afternoons and stay stunted. Resting spores survive in soil for many years.

manas.q: What causes clubroot and what does it do to roots?

children.note: Lime acid soils, improve drainage, rotate widely, plant only clean seedlings, clean soil from tools and boots, and use resistant varieties where available.
Yellow patches on the upper leaf with grey-white growth beneath, common in cool, humid nurseries. Space plants, ventilate and keep leaves dry.
Dark round spots with rings on older leaves and heads. Seed-borne; use clean seed, rotation and remove old leaves.
Pectobacterium bacteria turn heads slimy and smelly, usually after injury. Avoid wounds, harvest in dry weather and cool quickly.
Seedlings collapse at soil level in wet nurseries. Use fresh media, avoid overwatering and apply Trichoderma.
Opens the map on bacterial diseases, including black rot.
Opens the map on root rots and damping-off.
Opens the map on downy and powdery mildews.
Opens the map on blights and leaf spots.
Early weeds reduce yield, and cruciferous weeds carry brassica pests and diseases.
Wild mustard, wild radish and shepherd's purse host clubroot, black rot, diamondback moth and aphids. Remove them in and around fields.

manas.q: Why must cruciferous weeds be controlled around brassica fields?

children.note: Use a stale seedbed, mulch and shallow hoeing until the canopy closes. Herbicides are not allowed in organic production.
Opens the map on organic weed management.
Leafy brassicas lose quality fast; speed, shade and cooling matter.
Pick mature lower leaves regularly, leaving the growing tip and several young leaves so the plant keeps producing.
Cut when heads are firm, keeping a few wrapper leaves for protection. Late-maturing types can be stored for weeks in cool, humid conditions.
Tie or fold outer leaves over young curds to keep them white, and cut while the curd is still compact.

manas.q: Why are leaves tied over cauliflower curds?

children.note: Cut heads while buds are tight and green; once yellow flowers open, quality is lost. Then harvest the side shoots.

manas.q: When is broccoli past its best harvest stage?

children.note: Harvest in the cool morning, keep produce shaded and moist, and sell or cool it quickly. Keep broccoli away from ripening fruit, whose ethylene yellows it.
How organic brassicas are sold and what rules apply.
Kale gives small, steady income all year from local markets, which suits smallholders and urban growers.
Organic brassicas cannot receive synthetic fertilizers, synthetic insecticides or fungicides, or herbicides. Bt, spinosad, neem, copper and sulphur are allowed within each standard's limits.
East Africa uses the East African Organic Products Standard (EAS 456), India the NPOP. Participatory Guarantee Systems help groups sell certified organic vegetables locally.
Pesticide residues on leafy vegetables are a public concern because leaves are eaten soon after spraying. Clean, recorded production is a selling point; buyers check MRLs.
Most brassicas are sold locally or regionally; exports of fresh vegetables to the EU must meet MRLs and plant-health rules, with full traceability.

nodeData.note: How to grow onion and garlic organically: choosing day-length-correct varieties, nursery and planting, organic nutrition with biofertilizers, careful watering, thrips and white rot control, curing, storage and markets.

children.note: Onion and garlic are bulb crops of the genus Allium, grown almost everywhere and in daily demand, which makes them reliable cash crops.
Grown from true seed, usually raised in a nursery and transplanted. The bulb is made of swollen leaf bases.

manas.q: Which part of the plant forms an onion bulb?

children.note: Most garlic sets no viable seed and is grown from cloves, so diseases and viruses pass from one crop to the next in the planting material.

manas.q: How is garlic normally propagated?

children.note: Onion varieties bulb only when days reach a set length: short-day types bulb at about 11–12 hours, long-day types need 14 or more. Near the equator only short-day varieties bulb.

manas.q: Which onion type must be grown near the equator, and why?

children.note: Garlic cloves need a period of cool temperature before or after planting to form well-divided bulbs; in warm places they may give single round bulbs.
Red Creole and Bombay Red are common open-pollinated red onions; Red Creole is pungent and stores well. Several red F1 hybrids give higher yields but cost more seed.
ICAR-DOGR and NHRDF releases are widely used, e.g. Bhima Super and Bhima Red, Agrifound Dark Red and N-53 for kharif; for garlic, Yamuna Safed and Bhima Purple.
Alliums like cool weather while leaves grow and warm, dry weather while bulbs mature and dry.
Rain or irrigation at maturity gives thick necks, rots and poor storage. Plan planting so harvest falls in a dry spell.

manas.q: What weather do onions need at harvest time?

children.note: In Kenya onions are grown widely, including warm irrigated lowlands. In India the rabi (winter) crop is the main one and stores best; kharif onions are sold fresh.
Friable, well-drained loam rich in organic matter, near-neutral pH (about 6–7.5). Onion is sensitive to salinity and to waterlogging.
Allium roots are few, shallow and almost without root hairs. This is why alliums depend on good soil structure, steady moisture and mycorrhiza.

manas.q: Why do onions benefit so much from mycorrhizal fungi?

children.note: Do not grow alliums (onion, garlic, leek, shallot) in the same field more than once in 3–4 years; longer where white rot has appeared.
A healthy, hardened seedling or clean clove is half the crop.
Sow onion seed thinly in rows on raised beds about 1 m wide, in fine soil mixed with mature compost; mulch lightly until emergence.
Seedlings are usually ready at about 6–8 weeks, when they are pencil-thick. Reduce watering a week before to harden them.

manas.q: At what size are onion seedlings ready to transplant?

children.note: Dip seedling roots for 15–30 minutes in a slurry of Azospirillum and PSB, or Trichoderma/Pseudomonas, in shade, then plant the same day.

manas.q: What can onion seedling roots be dipped in at transplanting?

children.note: Fine, level beds with mature compost worked in. Close spacing (often about 15 × 10 cm) suits medium bulbs; wider spacing gives larger bulbs.
Plant large, healthy outer cloves pointed end up, a few centimetres deep. Discard small, soft or mouldy cloves.
Covering moist beds with clear plastic in hot weather for several weeks kills many weed seeds and soil pathogens before sowing a nursery.
Alliums need moderate, early nutrition; too much late nitrogen spoils bulbs.
Nitrogen and potassium are taken up most, with phosphorus and notably sulphur. Bulbs and tops removed from the field carry these nutrients away.
Sulphur builds the compounds that give onion and garlic flavour and pungency. Gypsum is an organic-allowed sulphur source.

manas.q: Which nutrient gives onions their pungency?

children.note: Work well-rotted compost or vermicompost into beds before transplanting. Fresh manure attracts onion and bulb flies and favours rots.

manas.q: Why is fresh manure risky for onions?

children.note: Late nitrogen keeps necks thick and green, delays maturity and cuts storage life. Finish feeding nitrogen once bulbing is well under way.

manas.q: What happens if onions get nitrogen late in the season?

children.note: Potassium improves bulb firmness and storage. Wood ash or compost made with ash adds potassium; use ash lightly on alkaline soils.
A legume green manure such as sunn hemp or cowpea, dug in well before transplanting, adds nitrogen and organic matter.
Use microbes with compost, not instead of it.
Coat onion seed or garlic cloves with Azospirillum and PSB, plus Trichoderma against basal rot.
Mix Trichoderma, PSB and mycorrhiza into compost and apply in beds before planting.

Pale yellow plants: nitrogen. Dieback of leaf tips: often potassium or water stress. Pale young leaves with poor pungency: sulphur.
Shallow roots need light, frequent watering.
Water little and often. Swings from dry to wet cause split and double bulbs.

manas.q: What causes split or double onion bulbs?

children.note: Moisture matters most during bulb enlargement. Stress then gives small bulbs.
Stop irrigating about 2–3 weeks before harvest so necks dry and bulbs cure and store well.

manas.q: When should irrigation of onions stop?

children.note: Drip saves water and keeps leaves dry, which reduces leaf diseases; straw mulch suits garlic.
Thrips are the number-one pest worldwide; good monitoring and early action matter.
Thrips tabaci: tiny pale insects hiding deep in the leaf folds, worst in hot, dry weather.
Silvery-white streaks and patches on leaves, later brown tips and twisted leaves. Heavy attack gives small bulbs, and thrips also spread iris yellow spot virus.

manas.q: What do thrips do to onion leaves?

children.note: Open the leaf necks of 10–20 plants across the field each week and count thrips. Blue or yellow sticky traps show when numbers rise.
Spinosad (a fermentation product allowed by many organic standards) plus neem oil reduced thrips and raised yields in an organic trial; Beauveria and overhead irrigation also help.
Avoid broad-spectrum synthetic insecticides: they are not allowed in organic farming, kill predatory thrips and bugs, and thrips quickly become resistant.
Maggots of Delia antiqua and related flies tunnel into bulbs, mostly in cool climates. Avoid fresh manure, rotate, and use fine insect netting.
Cutworms cut seedlings at soil level; beet armyworm larvae feed inside leaves. Hand-pick, use Bt or NPV products where registered, and plough to expose pupae.
Ditylenchus dipsaci makes garlic and onion bases swollen, soft and cracked. It travels in cloves: use clean planting stock and long rotations.
Eriophyid and bulb mites distort leaves and damage stored cloves. Use clean cloves and remove old crop debris.

Cutworms and armyworms in depth.
Leaf blights in humid weather, white rot and basal rot in the soil, and neck and black mould rots in storage.
Alternaria porri: small white sunken spots that grow into purple-brown oval lesions with rings and a yellow halo. Worse in warm humid weather and after thrips damage.

manas.q: Describe a purple blotch lesion on onion.

children.note: Stemphylium vesicarium: yellow-brown streaks on the leaf side facing prevailing wind, a major problem in India. Manage both blights with rotation, wider spacing, thrips control and copper sprays.
Peronospora destructor: pale oval patches with grey-violet fuzz in cool, humid mornings; leaves bend and collapse. Use clean sets, airy spacing and copper.
Stromatinia (Sclerotium) cepivora, the most feared allium soil disease.
Older leaves yellow and die back; the base is covered with white fluffy mould and many tiny black, poppy-seed-like sclerotia.

manas.q: What are the tiny black specks on a white-rotted onion base?

children.note: Sclerotia survive in soil for many years without any allium crop, so one infested field can be lost to alliums for a long time. Keep infested soil and tools off clean land.
Onion or garlic oil and allium waste make sclerotia germinate with no host present, so they starve; field trials killed most sclerotia. Bio-solarization also cut viability.
Roots rot and the bulb base turns soft and brown, often in warm soil. Rotate, use Trichoderma and avoid wounding roots.
Neck rot (Botrytis) starts at a poorly dried neck; black mould (Aspergillus niger) shows as black powder between scales. Good curing prevents most of both.
Iris yellow spot virus (thrips-borne) gives diamond-shaped straw lesions; onion yellow dwarf and garlic viruses build up in cloves. Use clean seed or virus-free garlic stock.

Onion is one of the weakest competitors among vegetables.
Thin upright leaves never shade the ground, and growth is slow, so weeds easily take over and can cut yields severely.

manas.q: Why are onions so sensitive to weeds?

children.note: Use a stale seedbed, hand or wheel hoe often while weeds are tiny, and mulch garlic with straw. Solarization helps in hot climates.
Curing is the step that decides how long bulbs keep.
When most tops (about half to three-quarters) have bent over at the neck and leaves start yellowing.

manas.q: What sign shows onions are ready to harvest?

children.note: When the lower leaves have browned but several upper leaves are still green, so the bulb wrappers stay intact.
Lay bulbs in rows with the tops of one row covering the bulbs of the next to avoid sunscald, for a few dry days.
Then dry under shade with good air flow for two to three weeks, until necks are thin, dry and tight. Garlic is often hung in bundles.

manas.q: When is an onion fully cured?

children.note: Keep bulbs dry, cool and well ventilated, in thin layers or ventilated stores raised off the ground. Remove sprouting and rotting bulbs often.
Pests of stored produce.
Onion and garlic prices swing widely, so storage and timing earn more than yield alone.
Kenya buys much of its bulb onion from Tanzania and other neighbours, so well-stored local onions sold in the off-season can fetch good prices.
India is one of the world's largest onion exporters; the government has repeatedly restricted exports when home prices spike. Dehydrated onion and garlic are also exported.
Use the East African Organic Products Standard or India's NPOP/PGS-India. Synthetic pesticides are not allowed; copper is allowed within limits.
Importers and supermarkets test for pesticide residues; thrips sprays are a common cause of failures. Organic and IPM onions avoid this risk.
Grading by size, clean dry skins and good packaging raise the price; garlic can be sold as clean bulbs, peeled cloves or paste.
